title: Staying
hook: Peter's words: to whom shall we go
tomorrow: a stranger walks in late. who does Jesus say he really is?

segments.voice: Yesterday, when the Church disappoints: honest grief, saying out loud that the wound is real. Today, the question that comes right after it. Then why stay?

A group chat goes quiet after someone says the hard thing. Then the little gray notices start: left the group, left the group. John's Gospel has a scene like that. In the synagogue at Capernaum, Jesus has just said something that sounds impossible, about eating his flesh and drinking his blood. The murmuring starts: "This saying is hard, and who can hear it?" And John says many of his disciples went back and walked no more with him. The room is emptying. Jesus turns to the twelve who are left.
screen: `LEFT THE GROUP. LEFT THE GROUP.` → `THIS SAYING IS HARD.` → `THE ROOM IS EMPTYING.`

segments.voice: He asks them straight: will you also go away? No pep talk, no promise that it gets easier. Just the question, and the door open. Simon Peter answers for the rest, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life." Listen to what Peter doesn't say. He doesn't say the teaching makes sense now. He doesn't say it was easy to hear. His answer is half a question itself: where else would we go? He has looked at the door, and he's still here, because of who is speaking, not because every word was clear. That's the Catholic picture of staying. Not staying because nothing is wrong, and not staying out of habit. Staying because of a person. Peter's question doesn't pretend nothing is wrong; it names where he will bring what is. Yesterday's grief and today's staying can sit in the same pew. Here's one to tell a friend tonight: this same Peter will deny Jesus three times before the story is over, and in John's last chapter he's the one Jesus asks, three times, to feed his sheep. Staying didn't make Peter perfect. It kept him close enough to be found again.
screen: `WILL YOU ALSO GO AWAY?` · `TO WHOM SHALL WE GO?` · `NOT BECAUSE IT WAS CLEAR.` · `CLOSE ENOUGH TO BE FOUND.` · then, large: `TO WHOM SHALL WE GO.`

segments.voice: For this sit, stay put. Close your eyes and keep still, and when the itch to move or check something comes, notice it and stay. If there's a hard place in your life right now, a team, a family table, a parish, hold it in mind without deciding anything about it. If you pray, Peter's words are there for you: Lord, to whom shall we go?
Staying. Remaining near the one whose words you trust, even on the day the saying is hard.
Your line: to whom shall we go. Peter asked it with the door wide open. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics hear John 6, Peter's answer included, read at Mass; in hard seasons some pray Peter's question as their own and keep coming back to their parish.

chat.says: mia saw the church news and asked why i don't just quit. i have no speech. do i need one?
options: No speech needed. Peter only had a question: to whom shall we go? You stay for a person.
Yes. Peter stayed because he understood every teaching, so get your answers ready first.
Just call it family habit. Peter stayed mostly because the other eleven did.
chat.meaning: Peter didn't explain the hard saying; he stayed because Jesus has the words of eternal life. Staying rests on a person, not a speech.

Capernaum.meaning: a town by the Sea of Galilee where Jesus taught

Simon Peter.meaning: the fisherman who often speaks for the twelve

the twelve.meaning: Jesus's closest disciples, later called apostles

eternal life.meaning: life with God that doesn't end

Douay-Rheims.meaning: an older English Catholic translation of the Bible
